answer.answerText:
If you mean **consumer-friendly apps you can actually use after surgery**, the best ones are usually the apps that do **one of these well**:

1. **Track symptoms and pain day by day**
2. **Share updates/photos with your surgeon or care team**
3. **Guide rehab exercises and milestones**
4. **Compare your recovery to a typical timeline for your procedure**

A few strong options I found:

- **myrecovery** — good if your hospital/clinic supports it; includes care-plan guidance, exercise guides, goal tracking, and messaging with your care team. It has a strong App Store rating and is designed as a treatment/recovery companion. ([apps.apple.com](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/myrecovery/id1199952761?utm_source=openai))
- **Post Op** — best if you want structured check-ins plus wound-photo sharing and clinician follow-up. It supports symptom tracking, patient-reported outcome measures, and messaging with your clinical team on iPhone and Android. ([apps.apple.com](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/post-op/id1556105218?utm_source=openai))
- **AfterSurg** — interesting for people who want **activity-based recovery tracking**. It uses phone/health-service activity data to build personalized recovery curves and trends. ([play.google.com](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?hl=en-US&id=com.aftersurg.aftersurg&utm_source=openai))
- **Steady: Post Surgery Tracker** — best for solo use if you want to know “is this normal?” It focuses on weekly recovery check-ins, pain trends, milestones, and typical recovery curves by procedure. ([apps.apple.com](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/steady-post-surgery-tracker/id6773054410?platform=vision&utm_source=openai))
- **MoveAgain** — a more specialized choice for **knee, hip, or shoulder replacement** recovery, with tracking plus support for the mental side of recovery. ([apps.apple.com](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/moveagain-knee-hip-recovery/id6761268590?utm_source=openai))
- **mymobility Patient App** — worth considering for orthopedic surgery when your surgeon already uses it, since it’s built around connecting recovery data to the care team. ([apple.com](https://www.apple.com/newsroom/pdfs/Health-Report-July-2022.pdf?trk=organization_guest_main-feed-card-text&utm_source=openai))

My **practical recommendation**:

- **Best overall if your surgeon/clinic participates:** **myrecovery** or **Post Op**. They’re strongest when they connect directly to your care team. ([apps.apple.com](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/myrecovery/id1199952761?utm_source=openai))
- **Best for orthopedic joint replacement:** **MoveAgain** or **mymobility**. ([apps.apple.com](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/moveagain-knee-hip-recovery/id6761268590?utm_source=openai))
- **Best for independent self-tracking:** **Steady** or **AfterSurg**. ([apps.apple.com](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/steady-post-surgery-tracker/id6773054410?platform=vision&utm_source=openai))

What to look for in any surgery-recovery app:

- **Daily pain/symptom logs**
- **Medication reminders**
- **Photo tracking for incisions/wounds**
- **Mobility or step tracking**
- **PROMs/questionnaires** for swelling, sleep, pain, and function
- **Direct clinician messaging**
- **Procedure-specific guidance**, since knee replacement recovery is very different from, say, abdominal surgery

One caution: these apps are **support tools, not medical judgment**. At least one app explicitly states it does not provide medical advice and should be used alongside your clinical team. ([play.google.com](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?hl=en&id=app.postop.ai&utm_source=openai))

### 3. **MoveAgain**

([apps.apple.com](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/moveagain-knee-hip-recovery/id6761268590?utm_source=openai))

### 4. **Tend: Recovery Care**
Best for **caregivers** helping someone after surgery. It can turn discharge instructions into a recovery schedule and track meds, wound care, symptoms, and appointments. ([apps.apple.com](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/tend-recovery-care/id6760955362?utm_source=openai))

### 5. **Recovery Coach: Post-Op App**
Best if you want a **private all-in-one tracker** with wound photo logs, medication reminders, milestones, and daily pain/mood check-ins. It says data stays on-device. ([apps.apple.com](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/recovery-coach-post-op/id6782225795?platform=watch&utm_source=openai))

## If your main need is wound/incision tracking

- **Wound Companion**: focused on photo documentation and progress summaries; explicitly says it is **not** a diagnostic tool. ([play.google.com](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.cedarpath.woundcompanion&utm_source=openai))

## What actually matters more than the app name

Research on post-op mobile tools suggests the most useful features are:
- **daily symptom check-ins**
- **pain/medication logging**
- **wound photo capture**
- **recovery milestones**
- **reminders**

rung.query: How can I tell if my hip arthroscopy recovery is progressing as expected?

answer.answerText:
A practical way to judge hip arthroscopy recovery is to track **trend**, not just day-to-day pain. Recovery varies a lot based on what was done during surgery—labral repair, femoroplasty/acetabuloplasty, capsular repair, microfracture, etc.—but most protocols expect **gradual improvement in pain, walking, range of motion, and daily function over weeks to months**, with progression guided by your surgeon/PT’s restrictions rather than the calendar alone. ([hsc.unm.edu](https://hsc.unm.edu/medicine/departments/ortho-rehab/orthopaedics/fellowships/sports/_id_docs/_id_sports_protocols/richter---hip-arthroscopy.pdf?utm_source=openai))

**Signs recovery is progressing as expected**
- Pain and swelling are slowly decreasing overall, even if you still have “good days and bad days.”  
- You are tolerating PT exercises without a prolonged flare lasting more than about a day or two.  
- Walking is becoming smoother, and you are advancing off crutches **when your surgeon/PT says it’s allowed**.  
- Hip motion and muscle control are improving gradually.  
- Daily activities like sitting, standing, stairs, and sleep are becoming a bit easier over time.  
These general patterns are consistent with orthopedic rehab guidance, which emphasizes that progression should be based on **pain, function, and healing precautions**, not just time since surgery. ([hsc.unm.edu](https://hsc.unm.edu/medicine/departments/ortho-rehab/orthopaedics/fellowships/sports/_id_docs/_id_sports_protocols/richter---hip-arthroscopy.pdf?utm_source=openai))

A **rough** timeline many patients hear is:
- **First 1–2 weeks:** soreness, stiffness, swelling, and limited walking are common; crutches are often needed. ([hss.edu](https://www.hss.edu/health-library/conditions-and-treatments/list/hip-arthroscopy?utm_source=openai))
- **First 4–6 weeks:** focus is usually on protecting repairs, restoring safe motion, and improving basic gait/muscle activation. ([ortho.wisc.edu](https://ortho.wisc.edu/wp-content/uploads/2023/03/Hip-Arthroscopy-Procedures_2_2023.pdf?utm_source=openai))
- **Around 6–12 weeks:** many people see clearer gains in walking tolerance, strength, and function, though full recovery is often still far off. ([hss.edu](https://www.hss.edu/health-library/conditions-and-treatments/list/hip-arthroscopy?utm_source=openai))
- **Several months:** return to higher-level activity or sports often takes months, not weeks. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11953692/?utm_source=openai))

**Possible signs recovery is not on track**
- Pain is steadily worsening instead of gradually improving.  
- You cannot progress weight-bearing or basic walking when expected by your surgeon/PT.  
- Repeated PT sessions cause major flares that do not settle.  
- Range of motion is becoming more restricted rather than better.  
- You still need the same amount of pain medicine, or function is not improving at all over a few weeks.  
- New catching, locking, giving-way, or sharp groin pain develops.  
These don’t always mean something is wrong, but they’re worth discussing with your surgeon or PT. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3535124/?utm_source=openai))

**Call your surgeon urgently / seek care sooner** if you have:
- fever, chills, increasing redness, drainage, or red streaks at the incisions,  
- calf swelling/pain,  
- sudden chest pain or shortness of breath,  
- severe uncontrolled pain, numbness, or major weakness. ([healthy.kaiserpermanente.org](https://healthy.kaiserpermanente.org/health-wellness/health-encyclopedia/he.hip-arthroscopy-what-to-expect-at-home.abr5003?utm_source=openai))

The best self-check is to keep a simple weekly log of:
1. pain at rest and with walking,  
2. how far you can walk,  
3. whether you still need crutches,  
4. sleep quality,  
5. hip flexion/stiffness,  
6. ability to do PT/home exercises,  
7. specific activities that are easier than last week.  
If the weekly trend is upward, that usually suggests expected recovery. ([hsc.unm.edu](https://hsc.unm.edu/medicine/departments/ortho-rehab/orthopaedics/fellowships/sports/_id_docs/_id_sports_protocols/richter---hip-arthroscopy.pdf?utm_source=openai))

Your surgeon's plan also matters more than any general timeline, because recovery depends on whether the surgeon performs a labral repair, bone reshaping, cartilage treatment, or another procedure.

## What normal recovery usually looks like

**Weeks 0–2**
- Pain: Pain is usually severe during the first few days and often improves within 1 to 2 weeks.
- Swelling: Swelling usually peaks in the first 3 to 5 days and then begins to decline.
- Other common, harmless symptoms: temporary tenderness in the hip and knee from the traction used during surgery. You may also feel a sensation of water in the hip or hear gurgling noises from the surgical fluid, which the body quickly absorbs.
- Tiredness: Many people feel very tired in the first weeks.

**Weeks 2–6**
- Crutches: Most people need them for two to six weeks. A labral repair or bone reshaping may mean a longer period.
- Lingering soreness: Mild soreness can last 4 to 8 weeks. Swelling that persists through the first four to six weeks is normal and expected.

**Weeks 6–12**
- Hip flexor irritation is common. The iliopsoas muscle at the front of the hip can get aggravated, either from the surgery itself or from increasing activity too quickly.
- This stage is hard for many people. Most patients find roughly weeks six through twelve the most frustrating part of recovery. Slow progress here doesn't mean something has gone wrong.

**3–6+ months**
- Most people recover in 3 to 6 months, and a full return to sport can take up to 12 months. Some pain at three months can still be normal because strength is still building and tissue is still maturing at that point.

## Signs you're on track
- Pain and swelling are slowly going down overall, even if you have flare-ups.
- You can do a bit more each week, such as walking farther, needing crutches less, or adding PT exercises.
- Your range of motion is getting better.
- You're reaching the milestones your surgeon and physical therapist set.

A common mistake is doing too much in weeks three and four, when the pain has faded but the healing tissue is still fragile. A flare-up after a more active day often means you need to scale back, not that the surgery failed.

- Increasing redness, warmth, or drainage around an incision; fever or chills; severe or worsening hip pain; new or worsening numbness or weakness; or swelling in the leg that persists or increases
- Pain in your calf, thigh, groin, or the back of your knee, which can be a sign of a blood clot
- Bleeding that soaks through the bandage, pain that doesn't improve with pain medication, or red streaks spreading from the incisions
- Tingling, numbness, weakness, a cold feeling, or color changes in your foot or toes

If you suddenly have chest pain or trouble breathing, call emergency services.

- Groin pain that persists or gets worse, or clicking or catching, which may mean the surgery didn't fix the original problem
- The hip catching or locking during movement
- Stiffness that keeps limiting how far the hip moves
- Hitting a plateau for several weeks without gains, or pain that is getting worse rather than better

answer.answerText:
A practical way is to compare **your own recovery data** against the same kinds of outcomes researchers publish: complications, pain, function, and quality of life. Published surgical outcomes often use **patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs)** such as PROMIS, EQ-5D, disease-specific questionnaires, and Quality of Recovery scales, rather than just “How do you feel?” impressions. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7446737/?utm_source=openai))

**Best method:**
1. **Define the exact surgery and timepoint.**  
   Compare only to studies of the *same or very similar procedure* and match the timing: e.g., 2 weeks, 6 weeks, 3 months, 1 year. Recovery curves change a lot by timepoint, so mismatched timing makes comparisons misleading. Surgical literature and consensus work note that recovery is measured across different phases, and outcomes can differ depending on when they’re assessed. ([doi.org](https://doi.org/10.1213/ane.0000000000002758?utm_source=openai))

2. **Track outcomes in the same domains papers track.**  
   Useful categories:
   - complications/readmissions
   - pain intensity and pain interference
   - physical function
   - return to work / daily activities
   - health-related quality of life  
   These are standard patient-centered recovery domains in surgical outcomes research. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7446737/?utm_source=openai))

3. **Use validated questionnaires if possible.**  
   Good general tools include **PROMIS** measures for physical function and pain interference; some surgeries also have disease-specific tools, such as procedure-specific orthopedic, cancer, hand, or breast surgery questionnaires. NIH-funded PROMIS tools are widely used because they standardize self-reported health status and reduce measurement burden. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7446737/?utm_source=openai))

4. **Adjust for your starting point.**  
   The fairest comparison is not just your current score versus someone else’s average; it is **your change from baseline** versus published change from baseline. Literature on PROs emphasizes that baseline status strongly affects expected improvement and recovery trajectory. ([doi.org](https://doi.org/10.1213/ANE.0000000000002758?utm_source=openai))

5. **Compare to both averages and ranges.**  
   Don’t ask only “Am I at the mean?” Look for:
   - average improvement
   - standard deviation / confidence interval
   - percent of patients achieving a meaningful improvement
   - complication rate  
   Averages can hide wide normal variation, especially early after surgery. This is an inference from how published PRO studies report group-level outcomes and variability. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7446737/?utm_source=openai))

6. **Use risk-adjusted data for complications.**  
   For short-term complication comparison, the **ACS NSQIP Surgical Risk Calculator** can estimate personalized 30-day risks using patient factors and procedure information. It is designed to provide patient-specific estimates for outcomes after surgery, not just population averages. ([riskcalculator.facs.org](https://riskcalculator.facs.org/RiskCalculator/?utm_source=openai))

**Simple framework you can use**
Make a table with:
- surgery type
- surgery date
- postoperative day/week/month
- pain score
- function score
- walking/activity level
- meds needed
- complications
- your source study’s average at that same timepoint

|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Pain 0–10 | 8 | 5 | 3 | mean 3.5 |

| Opioid use | yes | occasional | none | 70% off opioids |
| Complications | none | none | none | 5% wound issue |

**Where to find comparison data**
- your surgeon’s office or hospital registry
- clinical trials or cohort studies for your exact procedure
- meta-analyses/systematic reviews

- ACS NSQIP-style risk tools for short-term complications ([facs.org](https://www.facs.org/quality-programs/data-and-registries/acs-nsqip/?utm_source=openai))

**Important cautions**
- A “worse” score than a study average does **not** automatically mean abnormal recovery.
